newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine 91-day T-bill falls to 9.804 pct.
newsitem.headline: Philippine 91-day T-bill falls to 9.804 pct.

text.p: The Philippine benchmark 91-day Treasury bill rate on Monday fell to an average of 9.804 percent in the regular weekly auction from 10.159 percent last week, the Bureau of Treasury said.
The 91-day T-bill rate last stood in single-digits in September 1995.
Traders had expected the 91-day rate to tumble to a single-digit level after the Central Bank slashed its overnight borrowing rate last Friday by 0.25 percentage points to 10 percent.
A Reuter poll had earlier expected the 91-day T-bill rate to decline to 9.917 percent.
The withdrawal of the Central Bank's sale of three-month T-bills, which had a yield of 10 percent, also gave a cue to the market that the bank wants the rate to go lower, dealers said.
Other maturities likewise fell. The average of the 182-day T-bill rate skidded to 10.134 from 10.40 percent and the 364-day slid to 10.638 percent from 10.871 percent.
The auction had 16.620 billion pesos worth of tenders, of which 4.5 billion pesos were accepted.
A dearth of attractive instruments, brought about by the 20 percent tax on term reverse repos, had resulted in high liquidity among banks and pulled down rates, traders said.
"We're watching what the Central Bank would do next," said a foreign bank dealer, adding that the Central Bank may still cut its overnight borrowing rate.

However, "banks are currently cautious", the same dealer said. Traders said this was suggested by the amount of tenders on Monday, which were about 40 percent less than last week's 27.77 billion pesos.
Banks are either staying square or have started selling their portfolio of bills to post profits after rates fell sharply.

Traders said the Central Bank wanted interest rates to be lower in order to lessen the costs of doing business in the country. Speculation on the peso, however, could hinder the Central Bank's goal, traders said.
Early on Monday, the peso touched a low of 26.342 as some arbitrage money departed due to the low interest rates on the peso. Dealers said the peso is now recovering.
